description: We are three Master's students in Power Engineering at BTU Cottbus-Senftenberg, Germany. Participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, we aim to develop an innovative solution for the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge by analysing lunar surface conditions, solar illumination, power generation potential, energy storage requirements, and communication opportunities to identify suitable landing sites for future lunar missions.
summary: LUNARIS is a parametric mission-control dashboard that evaluates lunar south-pole landing sites by translating celestial ephemeris into actionable engineering decisions. Because the Sun hugs the lunar horizon at ~1.5°, power generation and Direct-to-Earth (DTE) communications are highly sensitive to local terrain. LUNARIS solves this by fusing topocentric Sun/Earth coordinates with an interactive 360° terrain mask to calculate continuous solar flux and battery State of Charge (SOC). The application outputs an immediate "GO/NO-GO" mission verdict. We developed a "Hardware Auto-Tuner" that calculates the exact minimum solar array and battery capacity required for survival, alongside a 360° Crater Rim Sculptor to test local topography shifts. By cross-referencing JPL Horizons data with our MATLAB/Simulink microgrid model, LUNARIS bridges the gap between raw astrodynamics and rapid, deterministic mission planning for the Artemis era.
details:
Project Details

What does your project do, and how does it work? LUNARIS is a web-based feasibility analyzer and physics simulator for lunar surface missions. It works by querying the NASA JPL Horizons API for 168-hour (7-day) state vectors of the Sun and Earth from specific Artemis candidate sites. The React frontend ingests this ephemeris and processes it through a lumped-capacitance power physics engine. We validated this web-based physics engine against a robust MATLAB/Simulink model. As shown in our documentation, the Simulink architecture connects a PV array subsystem to a Power Manager and Battery module, simulating real-world solar tracking and power distribution. The engine compares celestial elevation against a local crater horizon mask to determine binary illumination. It calculates net solar generation,subtracts baseline rover loads, and tracks battery State of Charge (SOC). If SOC drops below a safety threshold, the site triggers a NO-GO verdict.

What benefits does it have? It reduces site evaluation time from hours of manual geometric plotting to mere seconds. It explicitly quantifies engineering trade-offs and validates them against known benchmarks. For instance, our model aligns with validation data showing Malapert Massif achieves ~43.83% sunlight availability with 0% minimum SOC for baseline hardware, while Connecting Ridge (Site01) offers ~90.01% sunlight availability, maintaining a positive 8.38% SOC.

What is the intended impact? LUNARIS empowers mission planners to rapidly iterate hardware requirements for Artemis III. By linking mission dates directly to power survivability, engineers can instantly size their photovoltaic arrays and battery masses to survive extreme polar eclipses, preventing power starvation and thermal failure.

What tools did you use?

  • Engineering Validation: MATLAB, Simulink, Simscape
  • Frontend: React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS
  • Data Pipeline: Python, Pandas
  • Data APIs: NASA JPL Horizons API, NASA Moon Trek, LRO QuickMap

How is your project creative? We moved beyond passive 3D shadow visualization by integrating a deterministic Hardware Auto-Tuner. This feature uses a brute-force solver to mathematically size the minimum required rover hardware for any selected date. Furthermore, our validation approach is unique; we didn't just build a web app, we built a Simulink digital twin to ensure our time-series plots (PV Power, Power Manager switching, and Battery SOC depletion) accurately reflect physical hardware behavior during a lunar eclipse. Additionally, we built an interactive 8-sector 360° Crater Rim Sculptor, allowing users to manually raise or lower specific compass terrain to simulate topographical blockages.

What factors did your team consider? We considered the extreme grazing angle of polar sunlight, the libration of Earth in the lunar sky, and the critical difference between geometric visibility and terrain-masked visibility. Crucially, we factored in thermodynamic and electrical hardware limits. Our Simulink time-series analysis proves how a prolonged shadowing event causes PV power to drop to zero, forcing the Power Manager to draw exclusively from the battery,resulting in rapid SOC depletion.

Super Intelligence (SI) Usage Declaration In accordance with Space Apps guidelines, we acknowledge the use of Super Intelligence (SI) Large Language Models (Gemini/DeepSeek) to assist in generating boilerplate React UI component code, structuring Python data parsing scripts, and accelerating MATLAB syntax generation. No NASA branding or design elements were modified or generated by SI tools.
